# [Homepage](../index.html)

The theoretical exercises below are quite [difficult]{.orange}. In the
[exam]{.blue}, you can expect [simplified versions]{.blue}; in their present
form, most of them would be too challenging.

The data-analysis exercises, on the other hand, are broadly representative of
what you may encounter in the final examination.

:::callout-tip
Most of these exercises are adapted, sometimes with minor modifications, from
the textbooks @Salvan2020 and @Agresti2015. You may consult these textbooks for
additional exercises.
:::


## Data analysis

::: {.callout-note collapse=true}
#### `Seed` dataset - Partial solution: [`seed.R`](../code/seed.R)

The `Seed` dataset in the `MLGdata` package comes from an experiment designed
to assess whether, and to what extent, the amount of fertilizer affects seed
germination. Twenty seeds were used, and the following variables were recorded
for each seed:

- `fert` indicates the amount of fertilizer,  
- `x` is a binary variable equal to `1` if the seed germinated, and `0` otherwise.  

Import the data and then:

(a) Identify the statistical units, the response variable, and the covariate,
specifying the type of each variable (continuous quantitative, discrete
quantitative, nominal qualitative, or ordinal qualitative).

(b) Conduct an exploratory analysis to assess the relationship between the
response and the covariate.

(c) Using pen and paper, specify an appropriate GLM with the canonical link
function.

(d) Fit the GLM specified in (c) using **R**.  

(e) Report the estimates and confidence intervals for the coefficients. Provide an interpretation of the obtained values.  

(f) For each element in the output of `summary()` for the fitted `glm` object,
indicate which quantity is being computed and match it to the corresponding
formula in the slides.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### `Wool` dataset - Partial solution: [`Wool.R`](../code/Wool.R)

The `Wool` dataset in the `MLGdata` package comes from a $3^3$ factorial
experiment on worsted yarn. The response `y` is the number of loading cycles
until failure, and the three experimental factors are specimen length (`x1`),
loading-cycle amplitude (`x2`), and load (`x3`). The data were analyzed in the
classic paper by Box and Cox (1964):

> Box, G. E. P. and Cox, D. R. (1964). An analysis of transformations
> (with discussion). *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B*,
> **26**(2), 211--252.

For each of the three variables `x1`, `x2`, and `x3`, three levels were fixed:  

- Length: 250, 300, 350 mm (coded as `-1`, `0`, `1`)  
- Loading-cycle amplitude: 8, 9, 10 mm (coded as `-1`, `0`, `1`)
- Load: 40, 45, 50 g (coded as `-1`, `0`, `1`)  

Import the data and then:

(a) Identify the statistical units, the response variable, and the covariates,
specifying the type of each variable (continuous quantitative, discrete
quantitative, nominal qualitative, or ordinal qualitative).

(b) Using pen and paper, specify a [normal linear model]{.blue} for the logarithmic transformation of the response.  

(c) Fit in **R** the linear model from the previous point.  

(d) Assess the goodness of fit of the model and compare the usual standard
errors with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Discuss whether a
transformation of the response other than the logarithm might be more
appropriate.

(e) Write down the expression of the estimated curve.  

(f) For a test with length = 300 mm, loading-cycle amplitude = 10 mm, and
load = 40 g, obtain a 95% confidence interval for the conditional mean of the
log-response. Transform the interval back to the original scale and explain
which feature of the conditional response distribution it estimates. For the
same experimental conditions, obtain a 95% prediction interval for the
response.

(g) For the same data, considering the untransformed response and using pen and paper, specify a [generalized linear model]{.orange} with [Gamma response]{.blue} and logarithmic link function.  

(h) Fit in **R** the generalized linear model from the previous point.  

(i) Write down the expression of the estimated curve.  

(j) Report the estimates and confidence intervals for the coefficients. Provide an interpretation of the obtained values.  

(k) For each element in the output of `summary()` for the fitted `glm` object,
indicate which quantity is being computed and match it to the corresponding
formula in the slides.

(l) Evaluate the goodness of fit of the Gamma model.

(m) Using the fitted Gamma model, obtain a 95% confidence interval for the mean
response in an experiment with length = 300 mm, loading-cycle amplitude =
10 mm, and load = 40 g.

(n) Compare the results of the analysis based on the normal linear model with those of the analysis based on the Gamma model.  
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### `dde` dataset - Partial solution: [`dde.R`](../code/dde.R)

The `dde` dataset contains observations on a sample of $n = 2312$ pregnant
women and can be [downloaded here](../data/dde.csv). The dataset was also
analyzed in [Statistica I](https://tommasorigon.github.io/StatI/slides/sl_B.pdf).
The original data are described in
[this study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673601053296):

> Longnecker, M. P., Klebanoff, M. A., Zhou, H., and Brock, J. W. (2001).
> Association between maternal serum concentration of the DDT metabolite DDE
> and preterm and small-for-gestational-age babies at birth. *The Lancet*,
> **358**(9276), 110--114.

The variable `DDE` measures the concentration of DDE, a metabolite of DDT, in
maternal serum during the third trimester of pregnancy (in
$\mu\mathrm{g}/\mathrm{L}$). The variable `GAD` (gestational age at delivery)
records the day of pregnancy on which delivery occurred.

DDT is extremely effective against malaria mosquitoes and is therefore widely used in areas where malaria is endemic. At the same time, DDT may pose a health risk, especially for pregnant women.

[Research question]{.blue}. We are interested in the association between `DDE`
and `GAD`, particularly in estimating the probability of preterm delivery
(before 37 completed weeks, i.e., before day 259).

Import the data and then:

(a) Specify several reasonable models for the main research question. Select
the most appropriate one using predictive accuracy and diagnostic tools.

(b) Is DDE concentration associated with gestational age at delivery?

(c) Predict `GAD` for a woman with a `DDE` concentration of
$100\ \mu\mathrm{g}/\mathrm{L}$ and compare it with the prediction at
$0\ \mu\mathrm{g}/\mathrm{L}$. Note that the latter value lies
just outside the observed range and therefore entails slight extrapolation.

(d) Compute the probabilities of preterm birth for all the observed values,
namely
$$
\psi_i = \mathbb{P}(Y_i < 259 ; \bm{x}_i), \qquad i=1,\dots,n.
$$
Do they differ across models? [Hint]{.blue}: use `pnorm()` for a normal model
and `pgamma()` for a Gamma GLM. Pay attention to the parametrization.

(e) Estimate the probability of preterm delivery, $\psi$, at a `DDE`
concentration of $100\ \mu\mathrm{g}/\mathrm{L}$ and compare it with the
estimated probability at $0\ \mu\mathrm{g}/\mathrm{L}$.

(f) ☠️ [Optional]{.orange}. Obtain a [prediction interval]{.blue} for
`GAD` at a `DDE` concentration of $100\ \mu\mathrm{g}/\mathrm{L}$ and compare it
with the interval at $0\ \mu\mathrm{g}/\mathrm{L}$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### `Houses` dataset - Solution: Sections 3.4 and 4.7 in @Agresti2015.

What affects the selling price of a house? The `Houses` dataset is [available here](../data/Houses.txt) and comprises $n = 100$ observations on recent home sales in Gainesville, Florida. 

Variables listed are selling price (in thousands of dollars, `price`), size of house (in square feet, `size`), annual property tax bill (in dollars, `taxes`), number of bedrooms (`beds`), number of bathrooms (`baths`), and whether the house is new (`new`, with `1` = new and `0` = not new). The original source of the dataset is the textbook:

> Agresti, A. (2015). *Foundations of Linear and Generalized Linear Models*. Wiley.

Because all $100$ observations come from a single city, they do not support
general conclusions about housing markets. For illustrative purposes, however,
we treat them as a random sample from a conceptual population of home sales in
this market and analyze how selling price is related to the recorded
characteristics. The goal is to [predict the sale price]{.blue} from the other
variables.

Import the data and then:

(a) Summarize the data with descriptive statistics and plots. 

(b) Using forward, backward, or stepwise selection with all five predictors,
together with judgments about practical significance, select and interpret a
(generalized) linear model for selling price.

(c) Check whether results depend on any influential observations.

```{r}
Houses <- read.table("../data/Houses.txt", header = TRUE)
```

This exercise is intentionally left without strict instructions, so you can freely explore the data and develop your own modeling strategy. As is often the case, multiple approaches can yield reasonable results. 
:::

## Theoretical

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### Exercise A - Solution: [`exe_B_A.pdf`](exe_B_A.pdf)

Let $Y$ be a random variable with an [inverse Gaussian distribution]{.blue},
with support $(0, \infty)$ and probability density function

$$
p(y ; \xi, \lambda) = \left( \frac{\lambda}{2 \pi} \right)^{1/2}y^{-3/2}e^{\sqrt{\lambda\xi}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{y} + \xi y\right)\right\}, 
\qquad y > 0, \; \xi > 0, \; \lambda > 0.
$$
Show that this distribution belongs to the exponential-dispersion family and
identify its characteristic elements: the canonical parameter, the functions
$a_i(\cdot)$, $b(\cdot)$, and $c(\cdot)$, the dispersion parameter, and the
variance function.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### Exercise B - Solution: [`exe_B_B.pdf`](exe_B_B.pdf)

Let $Y$ have a [negative binomial]{.blue} distribution, representing the number
of independent Bernoulli trials with constant success probability
$\pi \in (0,1)$ required to obtain $k$ successes. Its support is
$S = \{k, k+1, \dots\}$, and its probability mass function is
$$
p(y; \pi) = \binom{y-1}{k-1} \pi^k (1-\pi)^{\,y-k}, \qquad y \in S.
$$

i. Assuming that $k$ is known, verify that this distribution belongs to the
exponential-dispersion family and identify its characteristic elements: the
canonical parameter, the functions $a_i(\cdot)$, $b(\cdot)$, and $c(\cdot)$,
the dispersion parameter, and the variance function.

ii. Using the properties of exponential families, recover the well-known relations  
   $$
   \mathbb{E}(Y) = \frac{k}{\pi}, 
   \qquad 
   \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{k(1-\pi)}{\pi^2}.
   $$  
iii. Show that the variance function is quadratic in $\mu$.  

iv. Does the distribution still constitute an exponential-dispersion family if
$k$ is treated as unknown?
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### Exercise C - Solution: [`exe_B_C.pdf`](exe_B_C.pdf)

Consider the general likelihood equations for a GLM:

i. Specialize the general formulas and re-obtain the likelihood equations for the binomial regression model (`Beetles` data with $p = 2$) presented in the slides, using the canonical link function.

ii. Specialize the general formulas and re-obtain the likelihood equations for the Poisson regression model (`Aids` data with $p = 2$) presented in the slides, using the canonical link function.

iii. Obtain the likelihood equations for a binomial regression model (`Beetles`
data with $p = 2$) using the [Cauchy link]{.blue}, defined as
$g(\mu) = \tan\{\pi(\mu - 1/2)\}$. This link maps $(0,1)$ onto $\mathbb{R}$.

[Hint]{.blue}: Parts i. and ii. require almost no calculations, only
substitutions. They are intended to familiarize you with the notation and the
general formulas. Part iii. is more involved; use the derivative of the Cauchy
link, $g'(\mu) = \pi/\sin^2(\pi\mu)$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### Exercise D - Solution: [`exe_B_D.pdf`](exe_B_D.pdf)

Explicitly derive the contribution $d_i$ of a single observation to the
deviance of a Gamma generalized linear model. Then write down the deviance
$D(\hat{\bm{\mu}}; \boldsymbol{y})$ for a sample of size $n$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### Exercise E - Solution: [`exe_B_E.pdf`](exe_B_E.pdf)

Let $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be independent random variables, with corresponding values
$x_1,\dots,x_n$ of a [univariate]{.blue} quantitative covariate. Consider a GLM
with [no intercept]{.blue} and $p=1$, i.e.,
$$
\eta_i = \beta x_i, \qquad i=1,\dots,n,
$$
under each of the following exponential-dispersion models, specified through
their mean-variance pairs:
  
1. $\mathbb{E}(Y_i)=\mu_i$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\phi$, where
   $\mu_i \in \mathbb{R}$ and the constant $\phi>0$ is known.
2. $\mathbb{E}(Y_i)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\mu_i$, where
   $\mu_i \in (0,\infty)$.
3. $\mathbb{E}(Y_i)=\mu_i$ and
   $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\mu_i(1-\mu_i)$, where $\mu_i \in (0,1)$.

For each model, use the [canonical link]{.orange} and:

i. Specify the statistical model in terms of the "standard" probability distribution and write the log-likelihood as a function of $\beta$.

ii. Derive the score function $\ell_*(\beta)$ and both the observed and expected
Fisher information.

iii. Derive the equation that characterizes the maximum likelihood estimator
$\hat\beta$, obtain a closed-form expression when possible, and give an
approximation to its sampling distribution.

iv. For a fixed covariate value $x_i$, construct an approximate $1-\alpha$
confidence interval for the linear predictor $\eta_i = \beta x_i$. Then derive
the corresponding confidence interval for $\mu_i$. Indicate in which of the
three cases these intervals are also [exact]{.blue} $1-\alpha$ intervals.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### Exercise F - Solution: [`exe_B_F.pdf`](exe_B_F.pdf)

Suppose that $Y_1,\dots,Y_{n_A+n_B}$ are independent Poisson random variables
whose means satisfy
$$
g(\mu_i) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x_i,
$$
where $x_i = 1$ for $i = 1, \dots, n_A$ (group A) and $x_i = 0$ for
$i = n_A + 1, \dots, n_A + n_B$ (group B); thus, $x_i$ is a
[dummy variable]{.blue}.

i. Show that, for the log link $g(\mu)=\log(\mu)$, the GLM likelihood equations
imply that the fitted group means $\hat\mu_A$ and $\hat\mu_B$ equal the
corresponding sample means.

ii. Using the likelihood equations, show that the same result holds for any
differentiable link function for this Poisson model, provided that an interior
maximum likelihood estimate exists.

iii. Using the likelihood equations, show that the same result holds for any
GLM of the form $g(\mu_i) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x_i$ with a binary indicator
predictor, under the same regularity condition. [Note]{.orange}: If the weights
$\omega_i$ are not constant, then $\hat\mu_A$ and $\hat\mu_B$ equal the
corresponding weighted sample means.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### Exercise G - Solution: [`exe_B_G.pdf`](exe_B_G.pdf)

In a generalized linear model that uses a [non-canonical link function]{.blue}, explain why it need not be true that  
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{\mu}_i = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i.
$$
Consequently, the response residuals need not have mean zero.

Then explain why, in a GLM with a [canonical link]{.orange} and constant weights
$\omega_i$, an intercept must be included for this equality to be guaranteed.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### Exercise H - Solution: [`exe_B_H.pdf`](exe_B_H.pdf)

When selecting explanatory variables for a model, why is it inadequate to
choose the model with the smallest deviance (or, for a linear model, the
largest $R^2$)?
:::
